questions.html: In-order traversing a tree resulted in $\text{E A C K F H D B G};$ the preorder traversal would return.

options.html: $\text{F A E K C D B H G}$
$\text{F A E K C D H G B}$
$\text{E A F K H D C B G}$
$\text{F E A K D C H B G}$

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 7)

$\text{Inorder Traversal} = left-root-right$

$\text{Preorder Traversal} = root-left-right$

$\text{Inorder Traversal} = E-A-C-K-F-H-D-B-G$

Now, as per option (C) $E$ is the $root$.

$\therefore$ Left sub-tree is empty and Right sub-tree inorder traversal = $A-C-K-F-H-D-B-G$

Now, $A$ is the $root$.

$\therefore$ Left sub-tree is empty and Right sub-tree inorder traversal = $C-K-F-H-D-B-G$

Now, $F$ is the $root$.

$\therefore$ Left sub-tree inorder traversal = $C-K$ and Right sub-tree inorder traversal = $H-D-B-G$

But as per option (C), if node $H$ is part of right sub-tree then node $C$ is also part of right sub-tree. This is contradicting to given right sub-tree inorder traversal $H-D-B-G$

Therefore, option (C) is not correct.

Now, as per options (A),(B) and (D) $F$ is the $root$.

$\therefore$ Left sub-tree inorder traversal = $E-A-C-K$ and Right sub-tree inorder traversal = $H-D-B-G$

But as per Option (D), if node $D$ is part of right sub-tree then node $C$ is also part of right sub-tree. This is contradicting to given right sub-tree inorder traversal $H-D-B-G$

Therefore, option (D) is not correct.

Right sub-tree preorder traversal, as per option A is $D-B-H-G$ and as per option B is $D-H-G-B$

$\text{Right Sub-tree Inorder Traversal} = H-D-B-G$

Now, as per both options (A) and (B), $D$ is the $root$.

$\therefore$ Left sub-tree inorder traversal = $H$ and Right sub-tree inorder traversal = $B-G$

But as per Option (A), if node $B$ is part of right sub-tree then node $H$ is also part of right sub-tree. This is contradicting to right sub-tree inorder traversal $B-G$

Therefore, option (A) is not correct.

Answer :- (B).

P.S. : We've to check option by option as for a given inorder traversal there is not a unique tree. Using preorder traversal we can find root and using inorder traversal we can find left and right sub-tree inorder. We've to recursively do this until contradiction is reached or possible tree is obtained.

Problem Statement:

In-order traversing a tree resulted in E A C K F H D B G; the preorder traversal would return...

Solution:

To solve this, we need to find which of the given pre-order sequences produces the given in-order sequence E A C K F H D B G.

Let's test the options by trying to construct a binary tree from the Pre-order (Root, Left, Right) and checking if its In-order (Left, Root, Right) matches the input.

Option A: F A E K C D B H G

  1. Root: F.

  2. Left Subtree (from in-order): Nodes E A C K. Right Subtree: Nodes H D B G.

  3. Next in Pre-order: A. This is the root of the left subtree.

    • In-order left of A: E. In-order right of A: C K.

  4. Next in Pre-order: E. Left child of A. Correct.

  5. Next in Pre-order: K. Right child of A.

    • In-order split of C K by K: Left C, Right (empty).

  6. Next in Pre-order: C. Left child of K. Correct.

  7. Right Subtree of F: Pre-order remaining is D B H G.

    • Root: D.

    • In-order split of H D B G by D: Left H, Right B G.

  8. Next in Pre-order: B.

    • Problem: B is in the right part of D's in-order sequence (B G), but in pre-order, the left child (H) must come before the right child. The sequence D B... implies B is the left child or the left child is empty. But we know the left child is H. Thus, this option is invalid.

Option B: F A E K C D H G B

Let's build the tree:

  1. Root: F. (Splits in-order into E A C K and H D B G).

  2. Next: A. Root of Left Subtree. (Splits E A C K into E and C K).

  3. Next: E. Left child of A. (Leaf).

  4. Next: K. Right child of A. (Splits C K into C and (empty)).

  5. Next: C. Left child of K. (Leaf).

    • Left side done. Structure: F -> Left: A -> (Left: E, Right: K -> Left: C).

    • In-order check: E -> A -> C -> K. Matches.

  6. Next: D. Root of Right Subtree. (Splits H D B G into H and B G).

  7. Next: H. Left child of D. (Leaf).

  8. Next: G. Right child of D. (Splits B G into B and (empty)).

    • Wait, check In-order: B is before G. So B is the left child of G.

  9. Next: B. Left child of G. (Leaf).

    • Right side done. Structure: F -> Right: D -> (Left: H, Right: G -> Left: B).

    • In-order check: H -> D -> B -> G. Matches.

Result: The tree constructed from Option B produces the exact In-order sequence provided.

Answer: B. F A E K C D H G B

Source solution 2 (score: 10)

In order to get a unique BT we need to know one of the given combination of traversals  :

  1. Inorder + Preorder
  2. Inorder + Postorder
  3. Inorder + Level Order

If we are known that given tree is full binary tree (i.e. binary tree where every node has either 0 or 2 child nodes) then we can also get a unique binary tree with the help of Postorder & Preorder traversals because incase of full binary tree every node has 2 child nodes i.e. atleast one node in either side of it unless it is a leaf node.

We can also determine a unique complete binary tree with the help of any one of the traversals because the structure of complete binary tree with n nodes is fixed and we only need to map elements to their locations according to the traversal given.

Please note that these are the cases when question only mention BINARY TREE and not BST because in case of BST we can also uniquely identify the tree with anything i.e. either preorder / postorder / level order because in ay BST we already know the default inorder sequence which is nothing but sorted order of search keys.

Final Summary :

In-order + ( Pre-order / Post-order / Level-order ) $\rightarrow$ Unique Binary Tree.

Pre-order + Post-order $\rightarrow$ Unique Full Binary Tree .

Any order whether In-order / Pre-order / Post-order / Level-order $\rightarrow$ Unique Complete Binary Tree .

Any order whether Pre-order / Post-order / Level-order $\rightarrow$ Unique Binary Search Tree.

PS : inorder for BST we already know as it will be sorted in ascending order.

questions.html: Suppose we have a complete binary tree, $\mathrm{X}$, that is not a heap, and we wish to heapify it. The obvious thing to do is just insert all nodes of $\mathrm{X}$ into a new binary heap $\mathrm{Y}$. This works, but it doubles the space requirement. Suppose we'd prefer to heapify in place. Which of the following procedures will convert $\mathrm{X}$ into a heap (containing all of the original values)?

options.html: Sink (heapify down) all nodes in level order (first the root, then its left child, then the right child of the root, etc).
Swim (heapify up) all nodes in level order.
Swim all nodes in reverse level order.
Sink all nodes in reverse level order.

questions.solution:
Answer: B, D

Source solution 1 (score: 6)

A.

 No. [Here and below, we assume a max heap, which we present as an array.] Consider $1,2,3,12,13,4,5$. This will bring $3$ to the top, instead of $13.$

B.
Yes. This is just what you do to add elements to the heap.

C.
No. Consider $1,6,7,2,3,4,5.$ This will leave $1$ above $4$ and $5 .$

D.
Yes. At each step, the current node will be the root of a subtree all of whose nodes, with the possible exception of the current node, will obey the heap property (inductive assumption). In this case, heapifying down will necessarily work, just as when you swap a (small) node for the root in the remove-first operation.

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

 

Correct Procedures

Option D: Sink (Heapify Down) all nodes in Reverse Level Order

This is the standard Build-Heap algorithm (often called Floyd's algorithm).

  • How it works: You start from the last non-leaf node (index $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$) and move backwards to the root. For each node, you call sink().

  • Why it works: When you call sink(i), the left and right subtrees of node $i$ are already valid heaps (because you are moving bottom-up). Sinking node $i$ ensures the entire subtree rooted at $i$ becomes a valid heap.

  • Complexity: $O(n)$. This is the most efficient way to build a heap.

Option B: Swim (Heapify Up) all nodes in Level Order

This is essentially the Incremental Insertion method.

  • How it works: You start from the root (index 1) and move toward the last leaf (index $n$). For each node, you call swim().

  • Why it works: When you process the $k$-th node in level order, you are treating the first $k-1$ nodes as a valid heap and "inserting" the $k$-th element into it by swimming it up to its correct position. By the time you reach the last node, the entire tree satisfies the heap property.

  • Complexity: $O(n \log n)$. While less efficient than Option D, it is a perfectly valid procedure to "convert" the tree into a heap.

Incorrect Procedures

Option A: Sink all nodes in Level Order

  • Why it fails: If you sink the root first, you are trying to move a value down into subtrees that are not yet heaps. Once you move to the children and sink them, they might move a value "above" the root's new position that violates the heap property again. A single pass top-down using sink does not guarantee a heap.

Option C: Swim all nodes in Reverse Level Order

  • Why it fails: Swimming a leaf node only ensures it is correctly positioned relative to its ancestors. However, swimming nodes from the bottom up does not account for the relationships between sibling subtrees or ensure that the "new" parents created by a swim operation satisfy the heap property with all their children.

 
 

Let's use a simple Max-Heap example. Suppose we have the following complete binary tree $X$ that is not yet a heap:

Plaintext

       10 (Root)
      /  \
     20   30
    / \
   40  50

Walkthrough of Option D: Sink in Reverse Level Order ($O(n)$)

This method moves from the bottom-up, starting at the last non-leaf node (in this case, node 20).

  1. Sink 20: We compare 20 with its children (40 and 50). Since 50 is the largest, we swap 20 and 50.

    • Tree becomes: Root: 10 | Left Child: 50 | Right Child: 30 | Leaves: 40, 20.

  2. Sink 10 (The Root): We compare 10 with its children (50 and 30). 50 is larger, so we swap 10 and 50.

  3. Continue Sinking 10: Now 10 is at the position previously held by 50. We compare it with its new children (40 and 20). 40 is larger, so we swap 10 and 40.

    • Final Heap: 50 at root, 40 and 30 as children, 10 and 20 as leaves.

Walkthrough of Option B: Swim in Level Order ($O(n \log n)$)

This method treats the process like inserting elements one by one into an existing heap.

  1. Node 10: Already a valid heap of size 1.

  2. Swim 20: 20 is greater than its parent 10, so they swap.

    • Tree: 20 (root), 10 (left child).

  3. Swim 30: 30 is compared to its parent 20. 30 is larger, so they swap.

    • Tree: 30 (root), 10 (left), 20 (right).

  4. Swim 40: 40 is the left child of 10. 40 > 10, so they swap. Now 40 is compared to its new parent 30. 40 > 30, so they swap.

    • Tree: 40 (root), 30 (left), 20 (right), 10 (leaf under 30).

  5. Swim 50: 50 is the right child of 30. 50 > 30, so they swap. 50 is compared to its new parent 40. 50 > 40, so they swap.

    • Final Heap: 50 at root, 40 and 20 as children, 10 and 30 as leaves.

Why "Sink in Level Order" (Option A) Fails

If you tried to Sink 10 first in the original tree:

  1. 10 swaps with 30.

  2. Now you move to the next level and Sink 20. 20 swaps with 50.

  3. The root is still 30, but one of its children is now 50. The heap property is violated at the root, and because we already "passed" the root in our level-order traversal, we never go back to fix it.

 

 

Summary Table

ProcedureOrderMethodResultComplexity
ALevel OrderSinkIncorrect-
BLevel OrderSwimCorrect$O(n \log n)$
CReverse Level OrderSwimIncorrect-
DReverse Level OrderSinkCorrect$O(n)$

Correct Answers: B and D

The Core Concept

When converting an arbitrary complete binary tree into a heap in-place, a procedure is only valid if it guarantees that every subtree satisfies the heap property by the time the entire process finishes. Let's analyze the two standard linear methods.

1. Bottom-Up Heap Build: Sinking in Reverse Level Order

  • How it works: We start from the last non-leaf node and move backward to the root (reverse level order). At each node, we call Sink (heapify down).

  • Why it works: When we are at a particular node $i$, its left and right subtrees are already valid heaps because we are processing bottom-up. Calling Sink(i) correctly bubbles down the value at $i$ until the entire subtree rooted at $i$ becomes a valid heap.

  • Time Complexity: $O(n)$ — because the majority of nodes are near the bottom and sink at most a few levels.

2. Top-Down Heap Build: Swimming in Level Order

  • How it works: We start from the root and move forward to the last node (level order). At each node, we call Swim (heapify up).

  • Why it works: This simulates inserting elements one by one into an initially empty heap. When we are at node $i$, everything before index $i$ in level order already forms a valid heap. Calling Swim(i) correctly bubbles the element up to its correct position relative to its ancestors.

  • Time Complexity: $O(n \log n)$ — because the majority of nodes are near the leaves and may need to swim all the way up to the root.

Analyzing the Given Options

Let's test each option to see if it correctly converts the tree into a heap.

  • A. Sink all nodes in level order:

    • Why it fails: If you start sinking from the root, its children are not yet heaps. Once you sink the root down, you move on to its children. However, a subsequent sink operation at a lower level can push a large value up into a position that violates the heap property with the root, but the root is never visited again to fix it.

    • Counterexample: Consider a simple tree where Root = $1$, Left Child = $2$, Right Child = $3$.

      • Level order: $1 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 3$.

      • Sink(1): Compares 1 with max(2, 3) = 3. Swaps 1 and 3. Tree becomes: Root = $3$, Left = $2$, Right = $1$.

      • Sink(2): No children, does nothing.

      • Sink(3): No children, does nothing.

      • Result: Valid heap, but let's look at a deeper tree: Root = $1$, Left = $2$, Right = $3$, Left-Left = $10$.

      • Sink(1) swaps with 3. Tree: Root = $3$, Left = $2$, Right = $1$.

      • Next is level-order node 2. Sink(2) swaps with 10. Tree becomes: Root = $3$, Left = $10$, Right = $1$, Left-Left = $2$.

      • Violation: The root ($3$) is now smaller than its left child ($10$), but the level-order traversal has already passed the root and will never fix it.

  • B. Swim all nodes in level order:

    • Why it works: This is the classic top-down heap construction ($O(n \log n)$ technique). As you move from index $1$ to $n$, every time you encounter a node, you Swim it up, ensuring that the array prefix from $1$ to $i$ always forms a valid heap.

  • C. Swim all nodes in reverse level order:

    • Why it fails: Swimming requires the elements above the current node to be organized. If you start swimming from the leaves up to the root in reverse level order, swimming a leaf up does nothing because its parents haven't been processed or organized yet. By the time you reach the root, Swim(root) does absolutely nothing since it has no parent.

  • D. Sink all nodes in reverse level order:

    • Why it works: This is the standard, highly efficient Floyd's algorithm for building a heap ($O(n)$ technique). By sinking from the bottom up, we ensure that every time we call Sink on a node, its left and right subtrees are already perfect heaps, safely establishing the heap property for the entire tree.

Conclusion

Both B and D are mathematically sound procedures that will successfully convert tree $\mathbf{X}$ into a heap containing all original values in-place.

Depending on whether this is a single-choice or multiple-choice question:

  • D is the standard, optimized method taught in core data structures (Floyd's $O(n)$ build-heap).

  • B is the alternative insertion-based method ($O(n \log n)$ build-heap).
